title: Component Inputs and Outputs
summary: Pass data into a component with input() and input.required(), send events out with output(), and offer two-way binding with model(), all as signals.
introduction: Components become useful when a parent can configure them and hear back from them. In Angular 22 both directions are signal-based: input() exposes a value the parent binds to, output() emits events the parent listens for, and model() does both at once so the parent can use the [( )] syntax. This lesson builds a small task list from a parent and a child component and shows the compile-time errors Angular raises when a required input is missing.
learningObjectives: Declare inputs with input() and input.required() and read them as signals
Emit events with output() and handle them in the parent with $event
Create a two-way bindable property with model()

blocks.text: `input()` declares a property the parent can bind to. It returns a read-only signal, so the component reads it with a call, `name()`, and can derive values from it with `computed()`. `input.required<T>()` has no default and must be bound by every parent; `input(defaultValue)` is optional.

blocks.text: A fixed string can be passed as a plain attribute (`name="Ada Lovelace"`); anything dynamic uses property binding (`[name]="second()"`). When `second` changes, the child's `name` signal changes with it and `initials` recalculates, with no lifecycle hook needed.

blocks.title: Common mistake: reading a required input too early
blocks.text: Leaving out a required input fails the build: `NG8008: Required input 'name' from component UserCard must be specified.` Reading one in the constructor or a field initialiser fails at runtime instead, with `NG0950: Input is required but no value is available yet`, because inputs are set after construction. Read inputs from `computed()`, templates, `ngOnInit` or later.

Two options are worth knowing. `transform` converts the bound value before it is stored, which is how `<app-card disabled>` can set a boolean: `readonly disabled = input(false, { transform: booleanAttribute });`. `alias` lets the template attribute differ from the property name: `input('', { alias: 'label' })`.

A child should not reach into its parent to change things. Instead it declares an `output()` and calls `emit()`; the parent listens with the same parentheses syntax as a DOM event and receives the emitted value as `$event`.

src/app/task-list/task-list.ts

blocks.text: The child knows nothing about the list; it only announces that *its* task should go. That separation is what makes `TaskItem` reusable in any list and easy to test on its own. `output<void>()` is fine for events that carry no value, and `emit()` is then called with no argument.

`model()` creates a writable signal that is both an input and an output: the parent can bind it with `[(checked)]`, the child can call `set()` or `update()`, and each side sees the other's changes. Angular wires the `checkedChange` event for you.

blocks.text: The decorator forms still compile and you will see them in older code, but the signal versions integrate with `computed()` and `effect()`, need no `OnChanges` hook and are what new Angular 22 code uses. The CLI migration `ng generate @angular/core:signal-input-migration` converts a project.

blocks.title: Smart and presentational components
blocks.text: A common structure: a few *container* components inject services and own the data, and many small *presentational* components receive everything through inputs and report through outputs. Presentational components are trivial to test and reuse because they depend on nothing but their inputs.

questions.question: To send the value `42` to the parent through `readonly selected = output<number>();` the child calls `this.selected.___(42)`.
questions.explanation: `emit()` fires the output; the parent receives the value as `$event` in `(selected)="onSelect($event)"`.

questions.question: Which declaration lets a parent write `<app-rating [(value)]="score" />`?
questions.explanation: Two-way binding needs a `model()`. A plain `input()` has no matching change event, and an `output()` alone cannot receive a value.

seo.title: Angular Inputs and Outputs – input(), output(), model()
seo.description: Learn Angular 22 component communication: signal inputs with input() and input.required(), events with output() and emit(), and two-way binding with model().
